title: Early Homo sapiens at Jebel Irhoud
description: Fossils at Jebel Irhoud show our species living in North Africa about 300,000 years ago.

title: Blombos Cave engravings
description: Engraved ochre from Blombos Cave, dated to about 75,000 years ago, preserves deliberately scratched geometric patterns. This entry concerns engravings, rather than the separate evidence for a roughly 73,000-year-old drawing.

title: Early occupation of Australia
description: People were established in Sahul, the ancient landmass of Australia and New Guinea, by about 50,000 years ago. Excavations at Madjedbebe suggest occupation about 65,000 years ago, although the timing of first arrival remains debated. This marker represents northern Australia, not a proven first landing.

title: Neanderthals disappear from Europe
description: Neanderthal populations disappear from Europe around 40,000 years ago, although regional timing is debated. The marker shows Gibraltar as a representative Neanderthal archaeological region, not a proven last population. Neanderthal ancestry survives in modern human DNA.

title: Chauvet Cave paintings
description: Lions, horses and rhinos painted on cave walls in southern France.

title: Monte Verde and the early peopling of the Americas
description: Monte Verde in southern Chile has long been interpreted as a settlement around 14,500 years ago. A 2026 study challenged the site chronology and prompted disagreement among researchers. The approximate map date represents the conventional interpretation, not a settled proof of the first arrival in the Americas.

title: Göbekli Tepe
description: Huge carved stone pillars raised by hunter-gatherers, before farming or pottery.

title: Farming begins
description: In the Fertile Crescent, people start growing wheat and barley and settling down.

title: Çatalhöyük
description: A town of thousands, with houses entered through the roof and painted walls.

title: Early writing at Uruk
description: Administrative tablets at Uruk preserve proto-cuneiform signs around 3200 BC. Early signs were drawn into clay; the familiar impressed wedge-shaped script developed over time. This is an early stage of writing, not a single precisely dated invention.

title: Egypt is unified
description: Upper and Lower Egypt become one kingdom under the first pharaohs.

title: Stonehenge begun
description: The first earthwork circle is dug on Salisbury Plain.

title: Indus Valley cities
description: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa have grid streets and covered drains.

title: Great Pyramid of Giza
description: Built for the pharaoh Khufu; the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.

title: Sargon founds the Akkadian Empire
description: Sargon establishes Akkadian rule over Mesopotamian city-states, conventionally dated from about 2334 BC. The location of his capital Akkad is not securely identified; the marker represents central Mesopotamia rather than a known foundation site.

title: Code of Hammurabi
description: A Babylonian king carves 282 laws into a stone pillar.

title: Thera erupts
description: A major eruption of Thera buries Akrotiri on Santorini and affects the Aegean. The exact date remains disputed; about 1600 BC is an approximate viewing date, not a precisely established year.

title: Battle of Kadesh
description: Egypt and the Hittites fight one of the largest chariot battles ever.

title: Chinese writing on oracle bones
description: Shang priests carve questions to the ancestors on bones and shells.

title: Olmec civilization
description: San Lorenzo in present-day Mexico is a major Olmec centre, known for its colossal carved stone heads. The marker represents the site during its early flourishing.

title: Bronze Age collapse
description: Around 1200 BC, several eastern Mediterranean kingdoms and trade networks collapse over a period of decades. The date and Cyprus marker represent a regional process, not one simultaneous destruction.

title: Early Bantu-speaking dispersals
description: Dispersals of Bantu-speaking communities began in western Central Africa roughly 6,000–4,000 years ago and continued over many centuries. Farming and, in later phases, ironworking spread through different regions. The marker represents the broad Nigeria–Cameroon homeland, not a single departure site.

title: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga
description: Pacific navigators settle islands no human had seen before.

title: Traditional date of the first recorded Olympic Games
description: Ancient tradition dates the first recorded Olympic Games at Olympia to 776 BC. The festival honoured Zeus, and the competition probably had earlier roots; this is not a securely documented invention date.

title: Rome founded (by legend)
description: Romans later counted their years from this date.

title: Cyrus takes Babylon
description: Cyrus conquers Babylon in 539 BC, incorporating the Neo-Babylonian kingdom into the Achaemenid Persian Empire. The marker locates Babylon.

title: Democracy in Athens
description: Cleisthenes' reforms give power to an assembly of citizens.

title: Nok culture
description: Nok communities in central Nigeria develop distinctive terracotta sculptures during the Middle Nok period, beginning around 900 BC. The wider Nok archaeological tradition is older. This approximate marker represents the terracotta tradition, not a securely dated invention of iron smelting.

title: Battle of Marathon
description: Athens defeats a Persian invasion force.

title: Parthenon begun
description: Work starts on the temple of Athena on the Acropolis.

title: Alexander's conquests
description: In eleven years, Alexander's army marches from Greece to India.

title: Kalinga War
description: After a bloody conquest, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka turns to Buddhism.

title: Qin unifies China
description: The first emperor standardizes writing, coins, weights and axle widths.

title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
description: Carthage's general leads war elephants over the mountains into Italy.

title: Han dynasty
description: The Han dynasty, conventionally dated from 206 BC, establishes an enduring model of imperial government. Its name survives in the term Han Chinese.

title: Zhang Qian journeys west
description: In 138 BC, the Han envoy Zhang Qian sets out from Chang'an for Central Asia. His journeys strengthen connections that later become known as the Silk Roads; these networks have no single opening date. The marker locates his departure city.

title: Teotihuacan grows into a great city
description: Between the first and seventh centuries AD, Teotihuacan develops into one of the largest cities in the Americas, with monumental pyramids and a planned urban layout. People occupied the valley earlier; this approximate marker represents its urban growth.

title: Caesar assassinated
description: Julius Caesar is stabbed in the Roman Senate on the Ides of March.

title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
description: Ash preserves a Roman town, down to the bread in its ovens.

title: Paper reported to the emperor
description: Cai Lun presents a papermaking process at the Han court.

title: Hadrian's Wall
description: From about AD 122, Rome builds a wall roughly 118 km long across northern Britain. The marker is one point along the frontier, not its entire extent.

title: Classic Maya era
description: Cities like Tikal flourish with pyramids, writing and astronomy.

title: Edict of Milan
description: The Roman Empire stops persecuting Christians.

title: Gupta Empire
description: The Gupta dynasty rises in northern India around AD 320, during a period known for major developments in art, literature and science.

title: Constantinople founded
description: Constantine moves the capital of the Roman Empire east.

title: Aksum becomes Christian
description: King Ezana of Aksum, in today's Ethiopia and Eritrea, converts.

title: Western Roman Empire ends
description: The last western emperor is deposed. The eastern half lasts another thousand years.

title: Aryabhata's astronomy
description: An Indian mathematician argues that the Earth spins on its axis.

title: Hagia Sophia completed
description: Justinian's Hagia Sophia is completed at Constantinople in 537. Its vast dome makes it a landmark of Byzantine architecture.

title: Plague of Justinian
description: The first plague pandemic is recorded in Egypt in 541 and reaches Constantinople in 542. The marker locates Constantinople, an affected capital, rather than the first outbreak site. This was not the earliest existence of the plague bacterium.

title: Tang dynasty
description: The Tang dynasty begins in 618, with its capital at Chang'an, one of the great cities of the medieval world.

title: The Hijra
description: Muhammad moves to Medina: year one of the Islamic calendar.

title: Umayyad conquest of Iberia
description: Muslim forces cross into Spain, beginning nearly 800 years of al-Andalus.

title: Baghdad founded
description: The Abbasids build a round city that becomes a centre of learning.

title: Vikings raid Lindisfarne
description: The attack on an English monastery marks the start of the Viking Age.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
description: The pope crowns the Frankish king in Rome on Christmas Day.

title: Diamond Sutra printed
description: A surviving copy of the Diamond Sutra bears a printing date of 11 May 868. It is the oldest complete printed book with a date; it is not evidence that printing itself began that year. The marker locates Dunhuang, where the copy was found.

title: Baptism of Kievan Rus'
description: Prince Vladimir adopts Orthodox Christianity.

title: Norse activity in North America
description: Tree-ring evidence dates Norse woodcutting at L'Anse aux Meadows to AD 1021. The settlement was active around this period; the evidence does not establish the year of the first voyage or identify Leif Erikson's crew.

title: Cahokia at its peak
description: Cahokia, near today's St. Louis, was a major Indigenous urban centre. UNESCO places its population peak, estimated at 10,000–20,000, between about 1050 and 1150. These are approximate period dates, rather than one precisely dated event.

title: East–West Schism
description: The Catholic and Orthodox churches split.

title: Battle of Hastings
description: William of Normandy conquers England.

title: University of Bologna
description: Bologna traditionally dates its university's origins to 1088. It is among the oldest universities in continuous operation; the date is a conventional foundation year.

title: First Crusade
description: European armies march to Jerusalem.

title: Great Zimbabwe
description: Stone walls built without mortar enclose a trading capital.

title: Angkor Wat
description: The Khmer build the largest religious monument in the world.

title: Mongol Empire founded
description: In 1206, a gathering in the Onon River region proclaims Temüjin as Chinggis (Genghis) Khan. The marker represents that region, not an established meeting site or the later Mongol capital at Karakorum.

title: Magna Carta
description: English barons force King John to accept limits on royal power.

title: Mali Empire
description: Sundiata Keita founds an empire rich in gold.

title: Moai of Rapa Nui
description: Islanders carve and move nearly a thousand stone figures.

title: Mongols sack Baghdad
description: The Abbasid capital and its libraries are destroyed.

title: Marco Polo's journey
description: A Venetian merchant travels to the court of Kublai Khan.

title: Polynesian settlement of Aotearoa New Zealand
description: Archaeological and environmental evidence places lasting settlement from East Polynesia around the late thirteenth century. These voyaging ancestors are central to Māori histories. The marker represents Aotearoa, not a proven single landing place or a traced canoe route. The end of this settlement window does not mark the end of Māori history.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
description: Mali’s ruler passes through Cairo on pilgrimage in 1324. Historical accounts associate his lavish distribution of gold with a fall in gold’s value in Egypt.

title: Tenochtitlan founded
description: Mexica tradition dates the founding of Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco to 1325. The precise foundation date is debated.

title: Ibn Battuta visits Kilwa
description: He calls it one of the most beautiful cities in the world.

title: Black Death
description: Plague devastates Europe in 1347–1351, with mortality varying greatly between communities. The marker represents Messina, one of the Mediterranean ports affected in 1347, rather than the full extent of the epidemic.

title: Ming dynasty
description: A peasant rebel leader drives out the Mongols and founds the Ming.

title: Zheng He's voyages
description: Huge Chinese fleets sail as far as East Africa.

title: Inca Empire expands
description: Around the fifteenth century, Inca rulers expand their state from Cusco across the Andes. The conventional date 1438 is associated with Pachacuti's rise, rather than a precisely dated beginning of all Inca expansion.

title: Gutenberg's printed Bible
description: Around 1454–1455, Gutenberg and his collaborators print the Bible in Mainz using movable metal type. The method helps transform book production in Europe.

title: Fall of Constantinople
description: The Ottomans end the Byzantine Empire.

title: Sunni Ali expands Songhai
description: Sunni Ali, who rules from 1464 to 1492, expands Songhai from Gao into a major West African empire. This marker locates Gao; the empire reaches its greatest extent under later rulers.

title: Columbus reaches the Caribbean
description: Lasting contact between Europe and the Americas begins.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India
description: The first sea route from Europe to India around Africa.

title: Mona Lisa begun
description: Leonardo starts the portrait in Florence.

title: The Reformation
description: Martin Luther's 95 Theses challenge the Catholic Church.

title: First voyage around the world
description: Magellan's expedition sails west; one ship of five returns.

title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
description: Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies take the Aztec capital.

title: Mughal Empire
description: Babur wins at Panipat and founds a dynasty in India.

title: Copernicus' heliocentrism
description: A book argues that the Earth goes around the Sun.

title: Tokugawa shogunate
description: The Tokugawa shoguns establish their government at Edo in the early 1600s. Their rule lasts more than 250 years, with prolonged internal stability.

title: Jamestown
description: The first lasting English settlement in North America.

title: Galileo's telescope
description: He sees moons orbiting Jupiter and mountains on the Moon.

title: Taj Mahal begun
description: Shah Jahan builds a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

title: Qing dynasty takes Beijing
description: The Manchu Qing begin almost 270 years of rule over China.

title: Peace of Westphalia
description: The Thirty Years' War ends in treaties signed in Münster and Osnabrück.

title: Cape Colony founded
description: The Dutch East India Company sets up a supply station at the Cape.

title: Newton's Principia
description: Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation are published in the Principia in London. The marker shows the publication city, rather than Cambridge, where Newton worked.

title: St. Petersburg founded
description: Peter the Great builds a new capital on the Baltic.

title: Industrial Revolution
description: Machines and steam power transform work in Britain.

title: Cook reaches eastern Australia
description: James Cook's crew lands at Botany Bay.

title: US Declaration of Independence
description: Thirteen colonies declare independence from Britain.

title: First Fleet arrives
description: British convict ships land at Sydney Cove.

title: Spain and Britain nearly fight over Vancouver Island
description: Spain seizes British ships at Yuquot. Both empires prepare for war before agreeing to share access to the Pacific Northwest.

title: French Revolution
description: The storming of the Bastille topples the old order in France.

title: Haitian Revolution
description: Enslaved people overthrow French rule and found Haiti.

title: Spanish America wins independence
description: From the crises of 1808 through the wars of the 1820s, Spanish colonies across much of mainland America gain independence. The 1808–1826 span is a conventional overview, not a single shared independence date. The marker represents Bogotá.

title: Battle of Waterloo
description: Napoleon's final defeat.

title: Tambora erupts
description: The largest eruption in recorded history causes 1816's 'year without a summer'.

title: Russia claims the coast to 51°N
description: A Russian decree claims exclusive trade and the Pacific coast north of 51°N—reaching into today's British Columbia. Britain and the United States reject it.

title: Stockton and Darlington Railway opens
description: The railway opens on 27 September 1825, pioneering steam locomotives on a public railway. Horse haulage also remained in use; this was not the invention of rail transport or an entirely steam-operated passenger system.

title: First Opium War
description: Britain forces China to open ports and cede Hong Kong.

title: Treaty of Waitangi
description: Māori chiefs and the British Crown sign New Zealand's founding document.

title: Oregon Treaty sets the border at the 49th parallel
description: In 1846, Britain and the United States agree to extend their boundary along the 49th parallel, while leaving all of Vancouver Island British. Expansionists had demanded a much more northerly boundary; that demand was not the final settlement.

title: The Pig War
description: Britain and the United States send troops and warships to San Juan Island after an American settler shoots a British-owned pig. The pig is the only casualty.

title: On the Origin of Species
description: Darwin publishes his theory of evolution by natural selection.

title: Russia frees the serfs
description: Alexander II abolishes serfdom.

title: American Civil War
description: The Union defeats the Confederacy and slavery is abolished.

title: Meiji Restoration
description: Japan's emperor is restored and the country modernizes fast.

title: Suez Canal opens
description: Ships can sail from Europe to Asia without going around Africa.

title: The telephone
description: Alexander Graham Bell patents the telephone.

title: Berlin Conference
description: European powers set rules for carving up Africa.

title: New Zealand women vote
description: The first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections.

title: Battle of Adwa
description: Ethiopia defeats an Italian invasion and stays independent.

title: Britain and France face off at Fashoda
description: British and French forces meet at Fashoda in Sudan in 1898 during rival colonial expansion projects. The confrontation becomes a diplomatic crisis; France withdraws its expedition.

title: Alaska boundary dispute settled
description: In 1903, a tribunal settles the disputed boundary between Alaska and British North America. The marker locates the Skagway area affected by the dispute, not the tribunal's meeting place.

title: First powered flight
description: On 17 December 1903, the Wright brothers make their first successful powered flights at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk. The first flight lasts 12 seconds.

title: Russian warships fire on British fishermen
description: In October 1904, Russia's Baltic Fleet fires on British fishing trawlers in the North Sea after mistaking them for hostile vessels. The incident causes a diplomatic crisis.

title: Einstein's miracle year
description: Working in Bern in 1905, Einstein publishes landmark papers on light quanta, Brownian motion, special relativity and the relationship between mass and energy.

title: Xinhai Revolution
description: Revolution begins at Wuchang in October 1911. The Republic of China is proclaimed and the Qing emperor abdicates in 1912.

title: World War I
description: World War I devastates Europe and other regions from 1914 to 1918. Nearly ten million soldiers die, alongside immense civilian losses. The marker represents one part of the Western Front.

title: Russian Revolution
description: The tsar falls; the Bolsheviks take power.

title: Penicillin discovered
description: Alexander Fleming notices mould killing bacteria.

title: Wall Street Crash
description: The Great Depression begins.

title: Salt March
description: Gandhi walks to the sea to protest British salt laws.

title: World War II
description: The deadliest conflict in history.

title: The Holocaust
description: From 1933 to 1945, Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators systematically persecute and murder European Jews. Six million Jews are murdered, chiefly during the war. The marker locates the Auschwitz region as one site within a continent-wide genocide, not the entire event.

title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
description: The only nuclear weapons ever used in war.

title: United Nations founded
description: The UN Charter is signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945. The United Nations formally comes into existence on 24 October, when the Charter enters into force. The marker locates the signing city.

title: Independence and Partition of India
description: India and Pakistan become independent; millions are displaced.

title: People's Republic of China
description: Mao Zedong proclaims the PRC in Beijing.

title: DNA's double helix
description: Watson, Crick, Franklin and Wilkins reveal the structure of DNA.

title: Sputnik
description: The first artificial satellite orbits Earth.

title: Ghana independent
description: Ghana becomes independent on 6 March 1957. This major milestone in African decolonization is marked at Accra; it is not the first independence of any country or colony south of the Sahara.

title: First human in space
description: Yuri Gagarin orbits Earth once in Vostok 1.

title: March on Washington
description: Martin Luther King Jr. gives his 'I Have a Dream' speech.

title: Moon landing
description: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon in July 1969, and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walk on its surface. The Earth marker shows the mission's launch site at Kennedy Space Center, not the lunar landing site.

title: Sydney Opera House opens
description: Jørn Utzon's shells become an icon of the 20th century.

title: Berlin Wall falls
description: Germans cross freely between East and West Berlin.

title: The World Wide Web
description: Tim Berners-Lee proposes the web at CERN.

title: Soviet Union dissolves
description: Fifteen republics become independent states.

title: End of apartheid
description: Nelson Mandela becomes South Africa's first democratically elected president.

title: September 11 attacks
description: Nearly 3,000 people are killed in the United States.

title: Human Genome Project completed
description: The Human Genome Project announces completion in April 2003. Its reference sequence covers about 92% of the total genome; remaining gaps are addressed by later projects. The marker shows the NHGRI research hub, not every participating laboratory.

title: Indian Ocean tsunami
description: One of the deadliest natural disasters in history.

title: The smartphone era
description: Apple launches the first iPhone.

title: Global financial crisis
description: Banks collapse and the world enters a deep recession.

title: Arab Spring
description: Protests spread across the Arab world, starting in Tunisia.

title: COVID-19 global health emergency
description: WHO declares a public health emergency of international concern in January 2020 and ends that designation in May 2023. Ending the emergency designation does not mean that COVID-19 or the pandemic ended. The marker locates WHO in Geneva, rather than the outbreak's origin.

title: Russia invades Ukraine
description: Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Webb telescope's first images
description: NASA releases the James Webb Space Telescope's first science images in July 2022. The marker locates the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which supports the mission; the telescope operates in space.

title: Needles with eyes
description: Eyed bone needles from Denisova Cave in Siberia are reported from layers around 40,000 years old in a 2024 scholarly review. Such tools allow thread to be drawn through material; they do not prove the precise form of the clothing sewn.

title: Dyed flax threads
description: Researchers report twisted and coloured fibres, identified as wild flax, from Upper Palaeolithic layers in Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia. The identification of the fibres has been debated. The approximate date represents the roughly 30,000-year-old material discussed in the original study.

title: Cotton in South Asia
description: Cotton fibres preserved by corrosion inside a copper bead at Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan, come from a grave dated to the first half of the sixth millennium BC.

title: Indigo blue in Peru
description: Cotton scraps from Huaca Prieta carry the oldest known indigo dye, older than any found in Egypt.

title: Silk woven in China
description: Silk textile remains from Henan are dated to roughly 5,500 years ago. They document early silk weaving in China; this marker represents the region rather than a proven first workshop.

title: The Areni-1 shoe
description: A laced cowhide shoe, stuffed with grass, survives in a dry cave in Armenia.

title: The Tarkhan Dress
description: A pleated linen shirt from an Egyptian tomb, the oldest woven garment known.

title: Ötzi's outfit
description: Ötzi dies in the Alps around 3300 BC. His preserved clothing and equipment include a bearskin cap, leather leggings and woven grass; the grass item's exact function is debated.

title: Tyrian purple
description: During the first millennium BC, Phoenician towns including Tyre are known for a prized purple dye extracted from sea snails. Earlier Bronze Age evidence exists elsewhere. This approximate marker illustrates the industry, not a known invention date.

title: Paracas mantles
description: Burials in the Peruvian desert hold embroidered mantles whose colours still look fresh.

title: Rome limits women's finery
description: The Lex Oppia caps how much gold and coloured cloth a woman may wear; it is repealed twenty years later.

title: Domestic silk production in Byzantium
description: Silkworm eggs reach Byzantium in the mid-sixth century, traditionally through monks described as smuggling them in their staffs. Domestic production develops under Justinian. Silk was already produced in several parts of Asia, so this did not end a worldwide Chinese monopoly.

title: Twelve layers at court
description: Women of the Heian court in Japan wear stacked silk robes, their colours matched to the season.

title: Quetzal feather headdress
description: An elaborate quetzal-feather headdress with gold ornaments survives in Vienna. Its association with Moctezuma is unproven. The date and central Mexico marker represent its early-sixteenth-century cultural setting, not a known production year or workshop.

title: Dhaka muslin
description: Bengal's fine cotton muslins become celebrated under Mughal patronage. Travellers describe cloth so delicate that it could pass through a ring; that is a historical description, not a measured standard. The approximate marker represents Dhaka's weaving tradition.

title: Kente cloth
description: In present-day Ghana, weavers make narrow patterned strips that are sewn together into kente cloth. Such cloth becomes a prestigious part of Asante court culture. This approximate seventeenth-century marker represents a developing tradition, not a documented invention year.

title: Hawaiian feather cloaks
description: Cook's crew is given cloaks made from the feathers of tens of thousands of birds.

title: The Jacquard loom
description: Punched cards tell a loom which threads to lift, an idea later borrowed by early computers.

title: The sewing machine
description: Elias Howe patents a lockstitch machine; within decades it reshapes home and factory work.

title: The first couture house
description: Charles Frederick Worth opens in Paris and turns dressmaking into designer collections.

title: Blue jeans
description: A patent for copper rivets on work trousers starts the history of denim jeans.

title: Wax prints reach West Africa
description: Dutch-made printed cotton finds its biggest market in West Africa, where it becomes local style.

title: Gandhi's homespun cloth
description: Indians burn foreign-made cloth and take up khadi, hand-spun at home, as a protest.

title: The qipao
description: The cheongsam becomes fashionable in Hong Kong in the 1920s among students, teachers, performers and other urban women. Its cut continues to change; Shanghai tailors later help shape Hong Kong's cheongsam tradition.

title: The little black dress
description: Chanel's short, simple black dress is compared to the Model T: one design for everyone.

title: Nylon stockings go on nationwide sale
description: Nylon stockings go on sale across the United States on 15 May 1940 and are an immediate commercial success. This is the nationwide launch, after earlier introductions and local sales. New York represents the national market.

title: The bikini
description: A two-piece swimsuit is shown in Paris and named after a nuclear test site.

title: Dior's New Look
description: Full skirts and cinched waists, after years of wartime rationing.

title: The miniskirt
description: Hemlines rise on London's King's Road and spread worldwide.

title: Chandrayaan-3 lands on the Moon
description: India's Chandrayaan-3 lander touches down on the Moon on August 23. The marker shows the mission's launch site.

title: Paris Summer Olympics
description: Paris hosts the 2024 Summer Olympics, with the opening ceremony on July 26 and closing on August 11. Some competitions begin before the opening ceremony.

title: Rubin Observatory reveals its first images
description: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile unveils its First Look images on June 23.

title: Milano Cortina Winter Olympics
description: Italy hosts the Milano Cortina Winter Olympic Games from February 6 to 22, 2026. Events take place across several venues; the marker represents Milan.

title: Artemis II flies around the Moon
description: Four astronauts fly around the Moon and return to Earth on April 10. The marker shows the mission's launch site in Florida.

title: Cleopatra VII rules Egypt
description: Cleopatra's reign spans the final decades of Ptolemaic Egypt. The marker locates Alexandria, not her whereabouts throughout the period.

title: Parthian victory at Carrhae
description: Parthian cavalry defeats the invading Roman army of Crassus near Harran. Rome's expansion encounters a powerful rival east of the Mediterranean.

title: Siege of Alesia
description: Caesar defeats the Gallic coalition led by Vercingetorix at Alesia, a decisive siege in the conquest of Gaul.

title: Glassblowing emerges in the eastern Mediterranean
description: Around the middle of the first century BC, glassworkers develop free-blowing, inflating molten glass through a blowpipe. The date is approximate and the marker represents the eastern Mediterranean, not a proven single invention site.

title: Battle of Actium
description: Octavian's forces defeat Antony and Cleopatra in a naval battle off western Greece. Cleopatra's reign in Egypt ends the following year.

title: Egypt comes under Roman rule
description: After the deaths of Cleopatra and Antony, Octavian annexes Egypt. The Ptolemaic dynasty ends; this point marks Alexandria rather than the extent of Roman control.

title: Monte Albán's second urban phase
description: The Zapotec centre in Oaxaca develops its ceremonial core, hillside terraces and water systems. These are broad archaeological phase dates, not construction dates for every monument.

title: Western Han China
description: Western Han rule spans 206 BC–AD 9. Its capital Chang'an grew into a great city of palaces, residential wards and markets. The marker locates the capital, not the dynasty's territorial extent.

title: Herrerasaurus
description: An early meat-eating dinosaur from Late Triassic Argentina. Its fossils help document the early history of dinosaurs.

title: Stegosaurus
description: A plant-eater with back plates and a spiked tail. Fossils occur in the Morrison Formation of western North America.
fossilRegion: Dinosaur National Monument region · Utah, USA

title: Diplodocus
description: A long-necked, long-tailed plant-eater. Adults and juveniles are preserved in the Carnegie Quarry at Dinosaur National Monument.

title: Iguanodon bernissartensis
description: A large plant-eater known from exceptionally preserved skeletons excavated from a coal mine at Bernissart.

title: Spinosaurus
description: A large sail-backed predator from North Africa with adaptations for life around water. Its lifestyle remains a subject of research.

title: Velociraptor
description: A small feathered predator from Late Cretaceous Mongolia, much smaller than its famous movie portrayal.

title: Tyrannosaurus rex
description: A large Late Cretaceous predator. The specimen SUE, found north of Faith in South Dakota, lived about 67 million years ago.

title: Triceratops
description: A plant-eater with three horns and a large bony frill, living in western North America near the end of the Cretaceous.

title: French Canada in New France
description: From Quebec's establishment in 1608 to France's cession of Canada in 1763, French settlement and the fur trade develop along the St. Lawrence through relationships with Indigenous nations. This is a period overview, not uninterrupted French control: English forces occupy Quebec in 1629–1632, and Britain conquers Canada in 1759–1760. The marker locates Quebec City, not the colony's full extent.

title: Champlain establishes Quebec
description: Samuel de Champlain establishes a French settlement at Quebec on July 3, a centre of New France on the St. Lawrence. Indigenous peoples had lived in the region long before the French settlement.

title: Ville-Marie: the founding of Montréal
description: French colonists establish Ville-Marie, the settlement that becomes Montréal, in present-day Quebec. Its founding site is at Pointe-à-Callière beside the St. Lawrence.

title: Great Peace of Montréal
description: On August 4, representatives of the Haudenosaunee and more than 30 other First Nations, together with the governor of New France, sign the Great Peace of Montréal. Indigenous diplomacy is central to this agreement.

title: Battle of the Plains of Abraham
description: British troops defeat French forces outside Quebec City on September 13. The city falls soon afterward; the struggle for Canada continues into 1760.

title: France cedes Canada to Britain
description: The Treaty of Paris ends the Seven Years' War and France cedes Canada to Great Britain. The marker shows Quebec, an affected place; the treaty is signed in Paris. French-speaking communities remain after the change of imperial rule.

title: Quebec Act restores French civil law
description: The Quebec Act restores French civil law for property and civil rights in the Province of Quebec, with exceptions. This helps explain Quebec's distinct legal tradition within British North America. The marker locates Quebec rather than the British Parliament that passes the act.

title: Quebec becomes a founding province of Canada
description: Confederation creates the Dominion of Canada with four provinces: Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The former Province of Canada is divided into Quebec and Ontario.

title: Quebec adopts the Charter of the French Language
description: Quebec adopts the Charter of the French Language, known as Bill 101, on August 26. The law makes French central to public life, work and education in Quebec.

title: Poverty Point: Indigenous earthworks and exchange
description: Indigenous hunter-fisher-gatherers build monumental earthworks in the lower Mississippi Valley and participate in long-distance exchange. These approximate dates describe the site's principal archaeological period, not the beginning or end of Indigenous life in Louisiana.

title: Hopewell earthworks in the Ohio Valley
description: Indigenous communities construct large geometric earthworks and ceremonial mounds in the Ohio Valley between about 200 BC and AD 500. Hopewell names an archaeological tradition, not a single nation with a mapped political border. This point locates Mound City, one of several earthwork complexes.

title: Ancestral Pueblo communities at Chaco
description: Chaco Canyon is a centre of Ancestral Pueblo ceremony, exchange and political activity, with monumental great houses and roads connecting sites across the region. The approximate period describes Chaco's regional importance; it is not the lifetime of Pueblo peoples, whose communities continue today.

title: Musqueam ancestors move to xʷməθkʷəy̓əm
description: Musqueam's account places the move of many ancestors to xʷməθkʷəy̓əm, the present community, about 1,500 years ago as the Fraser River delta changed. Around AD 500 is a rounded date for this movement, not an exact year or the beginning of Musqueam history. Earlier villages include c̓əsnaʔəm, more than 4,000 years old. The marker locates the present community, not the extent of Musqueam territory.

title: Haudenosaunee and the United States sign the Treaty of Canandaigua
description: On November 11, 1794, Haudenosaunee representatives and United States agent Timothy Pickering sign the Treaty of Canandaigua. The agreement establishes peace and friendship and acknowledges specified lands of the Six Nations. The marker locates Canandaigua, where the treaty was signed. This dates the treaty, not the founding of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

title: Fort Nassau opens for trade with Hudson Valley Native communities
description: In 1614, Dutch traders build Fort Nassau on the upper Hudson to exchange goods with Native communities. The Smithsonian places this trading house within a regional history of Mahican and Lenape exchange networks. The marker represents the Albany area, not Manhattan or a boundary of Native territory. The date records the trading house, not the beginning of Native trade in the region.

title: Pueblo Revolt: communities resist Spanish rule
description: Pueblo communities revolt against imposed Spanish religious, economic and political institutions, forcing the Spanish from Pueblo lands for more than a decade. The marker locates the Santa Fe area within a much wider uprising. Pueblo cultural traditions, languages and sovereignty endure beyond this event.

title: Haida village SG̱ang Gwaay enters the World Heritage List
description: UNESCO inscribes SG̱ang Gwaay on the World Heritage List in 1981. The Haida village preserves cedar house remains and carved memorial and mortuary poles that express relationships with land and sea. The date marks the inscription, not the creation or end of Haida culture. The marker locates the village in Haida Gwaii.

title: Kiks.ádi Tlingit defend Sitka
description: Kiks.ádi Tlingit fighters defend their fort at Sitka against Russian colonial forces. Following fighting and a blockade, the Kiks.ádi leave the fort on a survival march. This local encounter does not establish Russian control over all Tlingit territory or the disappearance of Tlingit communities.

title: Cherokee legislature establishes New Echota as its capital
description: The Cherokee national legislature establishes New Echota as its capital in 1825. The town becomes a centre of government and publishing before forced removal in 1838. This marker locates the capital in present-day Georgia, distinct from the later capital at Tahlequah. The date marks the establishment of the capital.

title: Cherokee Nation adopts a constitution at Tahlequah
description: On September 6, 1839, Cherokee delegates adopt a constitution at Tahlequah following forced removal to Indian Territory. The document establishes a framework of government for the reunited Cherokee Nation. The marker locates Tahlequah in present-day Oklahoma. This entry dates the constitutional act, not the whole history or continued existence of the Cherokee Nation.

title: Cherokee Advocate publishes in two languages
description: The Cherokee Nation establishes the Cherokee Advocate newspaper at Tahlequah in 1844. It publishes in English and Cherokee, using the syllabary developed by Sequoyah. Publishing is part of rebuilding the nation's institutions after forced removal.

title: Red River Métis establish a provisional government
description: During the Red River Resistance, Métis leaders establish a provisional government and negotiate the terms of Manitoba's entry into Canada in 1870. The marker locates the Red River settlement at present-day Winnipeg, a centre of the Métis homeland. These dates describe the resistance and negotiations, not the beginning or end of the Métis Nation.

title: Nunavut is created following Inuit negotiations
description: Nunavut becomes a Canadian territory on April 1, 1999, following Inuit negotiations and the 1993 Nunavut Agreement. Its public government serves all territorial residents; Inuit rights and title are also addressed by the Agreement. The marker locates Iqaluit, the capital. The date marks the creation of the territory, not the beginning of Inuit history.

title: Study documents Nenets herding resilience on Yamal
description: A 2009 study by Forbes and colleagues documents how Nenets seasonal mobility, flexible pasture use and local knowledge support reindeer herding on Yamal amid industrial development and environmental change. The date marks publication of the research, not the beginning or end of Nenets herding. The marker represents Yamal, not a migration track.

title: UNESCO proclaims the Sakha Olonkho epic tradition
description: UNESCO proclaims the Sakha (Yakut) Olonkho epic tradition a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005. Sung poetry and spoken storytelling transmit knowledge and beliefs. The tradition is later inscribed on the Representative List in 2008. This entry dates the 2005 recognition, not the origins or duration of the much older tradition.

title: Beringia National Park is established in Chukchi and Yupik homelands
description: Beringia National Park is established in eastern Chukotka on January 17, 2013. It lies in Chukchi and Yupik homelands, where local knowledge and land and sea practices shape the cultural landscape. This dates the park's establishment, not either people's origins. These communities must not be treated as labels for all Ice Age migrants.

title: Saami Council is founded for cross-border Sámi cooperation
description: The Saami Council is founded in 1956 to support Sámi cooperation across national borders. Sámi homelands extend across what are now Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia. The date marks the organization's founding, not the beginning of Sámi history. The marker represents Sápmi, not a council headquarters or a territorial boundary.

title: Traditional Ainu dance receives UNESCO inscription
description: UNESCO inscribes traditional Ainu dance on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009. Ainu preservation associations in Hokkaido transmit ceremonial and everyday dance as living cultural knowledge. The date marks inscription, not the beginning or duration of Ainu culture. The marker represents Hokkaido rather than all Ainu homelands.

title: Early Gunditjmara aquaculture at Budj Bim
description: Gunditjmara people develop channels, weirs and ponds to manage and harvest kooyang, short-finned eels, in south-eastern Australia. UNESCO describes at least 6,600 years of landscape engineering. Around 4500 BC is a rounded marker for early aquaculture evidence, not a known single construction year. The relationship with Country and the engineering tradition continue beyond this early milestone.

title: Tsodilo sacred landscape enters the World Heritage List
description: UNESCO inscribes Tsodilo on the World Heritage List in 2001. San and Hambukushu communities revere the hills as a sacred landscape. The rock art and archaeological record span many periods and cannot all be assigned to one present-day people. This date marks the inscription, not the beginning of the communities' presence or beliefs.

title: UNESCO proclaims Wajãpi oral and graphic expressions
description: UNESCO proclaims Wajãpi oral and graphic expressions a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003. Wajãpi communities in Amapá transmit knowledge through oral traditions and kusiwa graphic expression. The practice is later inscribed on the Representative List in 2008. This entry dates the 2003 proclamation, not the beginning or duration of the tradition.

title: Q’eswachaka bridge-renewal knowledge receives UNESCO inscription
description: UNESCO inscribes the knowledge, skills and rituals of renewing the Q’eswachaka rope bridge in 2013. Four Quechua-speaking communities carry out the collective work over the Apurímac River. This dates the recognition, not the beginning of Quechua history or every annual bridge renewal.

title: People at Yana in Arctic Siberia
description: Yana Rhinoceros Horn Site preserves evidence of people in northeastern Siberia around 31,600 calibrated years before present. The BC map date is rounded from that age, with present conventionally AD 1950. The find demonstrates human presence at Yana; it does not prove a direct journey from this site to Alaska or identify its inhabitants as any modern nation.

title: Human footprints at White Sands
description: Human footprints at White Sands are dated to roughly 23,000–21,000 years ago. Independent pollen radiocarbon and sediment luminescence dating published in 2023 support the original chronology. The rounded BC interval shows evidence of people south of the ice sheets during the Last Glacial Maximum; the footprints do not reveal the route they took to reach this place.

title: Early occupation at Swan Point, Alaska
description: A peer-reviewed synthesis dates Swan Point's archaeological record to about 14,200 calibrated years before present. The rounded BC marker represents an early dated occupation, not the first arrival of all people in Alaska or proof of a particular migration route.

title: Ancient Beringian lives at Upward Sun River
description: Burials at Upward Sun River in Alaska date to about 11,500 calibrated years before present. Research on diet provides evidence of life in eastern Beringia; separate genomic studies inform population history. The rounded BC marker locates this evidence, not an observed crossing of the land bridge or a claim that these individuals founded a present-day nation.

title: Smallpox vaccine: Jenner’s experiment
description: In Berkeley, England, Edward Jenner uses cowpox material to inoculate James Phipps against smallpox in 1796. This becomes a landmark in vaccination; variolation and earlier cowpox experiments preceded it. The marker locates Berkeley.

title: Rabies vaccine: successful post-exposure treatment
description: In Paris, Louis Pasteur’s team and physician Jacques Joseph Grancher give Joseph Meister a course of rabies vaccinations after a dog bite in July 1885. Meister survives. This records a successful post-exposure treatment, not a cure for established symptomatic rabies.

title: BCG tuberculosis vaccine first used in humans
description: The BCG vaccine developed by Albert Calmette and Camille Guérin is first given to a human infant in Paris in 1921. This marks the first human use of their tuberculosis vaccine after years of laboratory development.

title: Influenza vaccine approved for US military use
description: An influenza vaccine developed through research led by Thomas Francis Jr and Jonas Salk is approved for US military use by 1945; civilian approval follows in 1946. The Ann Arbor marker represents their University of Michigan research connection, not every development or production site.

title: Salk polio vaccine trial results announced
description: On 12 April 1955 in Ann Arbor, Thomas Francis Jr announces that field trials show Jonas Salk’s inactivated polio vaccine works. This public milestone follows years of development and the large 1954 trial; 1955 is not the beginning of polio research.

title: Measles vaccine licensed in the United States
description: John Enders and colleagues’ Edmonston-B measles vaccine is licensed in the United States in 1963. An improved vaccine follows in 1968. The Boston marker represents the research team’s location, not a worldwide approval date.

title: Combined MMR vaccine licensed
description: A combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is licensed in the United States in 1971. The individual vaccines already existed. The Philadelphia-area marker represents Maurice Hilleman’s associated vaccine research region, not all manufacturing sites.

title: Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine licensed
description: The United States licenses a hepatitis B vaccine made using recombinant DNA technology in 1986. It follows an earlier plasma-derived vaccine licensed in 1981. The marker represents the US regulator’s Washington-area location, not a single invention site.

title: First HPV vaccine approved in the United States
description: The FDA approves Gardasil in June 2006, the first licensed human papillomavirus vaccine. It prevents infections with selected HPV types linked to cervical cancer and other disease. The Washington-area marker represents the US approval, not every contributing laboratory.

title: mRNA COVID-19 vaccine authorised in the UK
description: On 2 December 2020, the UK regulator authorises the Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. This mRNA vaccine milestone builds on decades of research. The London marker represents the regulatory decision, not the locations of all researchers or trials.

title: WHO recommends the first malaria vaccine
description: On 6 October 2021, WHO recommends widespread use of the RTS,S malaria vaccine for children in regions with moderate to high P. falciparum transmission. The recommendation draws on pilot programmes in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi. The Geneva marker locates WHO’s announcement, not the vaccine’s invention.

title: The stethoscope is invented
description: René Laennec develops the stethoscope in 1816, initially using a rolled paper tube to listen to a patient’s chest. This medical instrument helps doctors hear internal sounds. The marker locates Paris, where Laennec worked.

title: Ether anaesthesia publicly demonstrated
description: On 16 October 1846 at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, William T. G. Morton administers ether during an operation by John Collins Warren. The successful public demonstration helps transform surgery. Earlier anaesthetic experiments and operations preceded it.

title: Semmelweis introduces clinical hand disinfection
description: In May 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis introduces hand disinfection with a chlorinated solution in a Vienna maternity clinic. Deaths from puerperal fever fall sharply. This medical infection-control milestone concerns clinical disinfection, not the invention of washing hands.

title: Lister publishes antiseptic surgery results
description: Joseph Lister publishes results of his antiseptic surgical methods in 1867 after experiments in Glasgow using carbolic acid to reduce wound infection. This publication milestone helps establish infection prevention in surgery; his clinical experiments began earlier.

title: X-rays discovered
description: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovers X-rays in Würzburg in 1895. The radiation makes it possible to image structures inside the body and soon becomes a major medical diagnostic tool. This date marks the discovery, not the invention of every later X-ray machine.

title: Human blood groups explained
description: Karl Landsteiner reports distinct human blood groups in 1901, helping explain why mixing blood can cause red cells to clump. His work lays foundations for safer blood transfusion. The Vienna marker represents his research; later work completes the familiar ABO system.

title: Insulin successfully treats a diabetes patient
description: At Toronto General Hospital in January 1922, Leonard Thompson receives pancreatic extracts developed by the Toronto insulin team. After an initial injection on 11 January, James Collip’s more purified extract produces a dramatic improvement on 23 January. The medical breakthrough follows the team’s 1921 research.

title: First lasting successful human kidney transplant
description: In Boston in 1954, Joseph Murray and colleagues transplant a kidney between identical twins at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital. Genetic identity helps avoid rejection. This medical milestone demonstrates lasting success after earlier transplant attempts; it does not solve rejection for unrelated donors.

title: First fully implanted pacemaker
description: In 1958 in Stockholm, surgeon Åke Senning implants a pacemaker designed by engineer Rune Elmqvist. This medical milestone places the pacing system inside the body; external cardiac pacemakers had already been used.

title: First human-to-human heart transplant
description: On 3 December 1967, Christiaan Barnard and a team at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town perform the first human-to-human heart transplant. This medical operation opens a new field, although the first recipient survives only 18 days.

title: First clinical CT scan
description: On 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley Hospital in Wimbledon, Godfrey Hounsfield and radiologist Jamie Ambrose perform the first CT scan on a patient: a brain scan. This medical imaging milestone follows earlier mathematical and engineering development.

title: Artemisinin isolated for malaria research
description: In 1972, Tu Youyou’s team isolates the antimalarial compound later named artemisinin from sweet wormwood. This medical discovery builds on earlier extract research and leads to new malaria medicines. The Beijing marker represents her research institute, not every clinical trial site.

title: Lauterbur publishes early MRI images
description: Paul Lauterbur publishes a method for producing images using nuclear magnetic resonance in 1973, following research at Stony Brook. This medical imaging foundation helps make MRI possible; it is not the date of the first routine hospital MRI service.

title: First birth following IVF
description: Louise Brown is born in Oldham on 25 July 1978 following in vitro fertilisation developed through work by Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe and their collaborators. This medical milestone is the first live birth after IVF, rather than the first laboratory fertilisation experiment.

title: First cholera pandemic begins
description: In 1817, documented pandemic spread carries cholera beyond its longstanding home in Bengal. Successive waves make it a global public-health threat. The Kolkata-area marker represents Bengal, not a proven first infected person or the disease’s full reach. This entry marks the pandemic’s onset.

title: Third plague pandemic: Hong Kong outbreak
description: Hong Kong suffers a major plague outbreak in 1894 during the third plague pandemic. Alexandre Yersin investigates and identifies the plague bacterium there. The marker locates this outbreak and research milestone, not the pandemic’s earlier origin or full duration.

title: 1918 influenza pandemic (Spanish flu)
description: An H1N1 influenza pandemic spreads worldwide in 1918–1919, causing enormous mortality, including among young adults. Its geographical origin remains uncertain. The Kansas marker represents early US military outbreaks, not a proven origin; the name Spanish flu does not establish an origin in Spain.

title: 1957–1958 influenza pandemic (Asian flu)
description: A new influenza A(H2N2) virus triggers a pandemic in 1957–1958. Early reports include Singapore in February 1957, followed by Hong Kong and other countries. The Singapore marker locates an early reporting site, not the entire pandemic or a proven evolutionary origin.

title: Seventh cholera pandemic begins
description: The seventh cholera pandemic, caused by the El Tor lineage, begins in Sulawesi, Indonesia, in 1961 and later spreads across continents. The marker represents Sulawesi. This entry dates the onset; it does not claim that the pandemic ended in 1961.

title: 1968 influenza pandemic (Hong Kong flu)
description: Influenza A(H3N2) causes a pandemic first recognised in Hong Kong in 1968. Waves affect different countries at different times through 1970. The marker locates Hong Kong, not the full area affected. The viewing interval summarises these waves rather than the end of H3N2 circulation.

title: HIV/AIDS pandemic: first recognised AIDS reports
description: In June 1981, the CDC reports unusual pneumonia in five men in Los Angeles, an early recognition of what becomes known as AIDS. HIV had circulated before these reports. The Los Angeles marker locates the reported cases, not the origin of HIV or the beginning of every infection in the global pandemic.

title: 2009–2010 H1N1 influenza pandemic (swine flu)
description: A new influenza A(H1N1) virus spreads globally in 2009–2010. The Geneva marker represents WHO’s international pandemic response, not a proven place of origin. The pandemic interval does not imply that the virus disappears: descendants continue to circulate as seasonal influenza.

title: Smallpox declared eradicated worldwide
description: The World Health Assembly declares smallpox eradicated in 1980 after international vaccination and surveillance campaigns. The Geneva marker represents the declaration. This public-health achievement follows Jenner’s 1796 experiment and generations of vaccine development and coordinated work.
